meta.title: Who really said "I am a slow walker, but I never walk back"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Lincoln as his reply on the Emancipation Proclamation; it surfaces in an 1864 newspaper but no source in his own writings pins it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I am a slow walker, but I never walk back'?
meta.ogDescription: An 1864 newspaper reports it as Lincoln's reply on emancipation. Early and in-character, but no primary Lincoln document confirms it.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1809–1865 · 16th U.S. president; the line first appears in print in January 1864
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Lincoln, and credited early: the words surface in the press in January 1864 ↗ as his reply when asked whether the Emancipation Proclamation was a finality, and they square with his incremental-but-unwavering temperament — but the line survives only as a second-hand newspaper anecdote, with no version in Lincoln’s own letters or speeches to pin it.

source.heading: An 1864 wartime newspaper item

docMeta.dd: “Gleanings from the Mails,” Daily Commercial Register (Sandusky, Ohio)
Lincoln’s reply when asked if the Emancipation Proclamation was a finality
Contemporaneous press attribution — not found in Lincoln’s own writings

source.excerpt: Mr. Lincoln, when asked recently if the emancipation proclamation was a finality, replied—‘I am a slow walker, but I never walk back.’
trail: The earliest known printing is a wartime newspaper item: the Daily Commercial Register of Sandusky, Ohio (14 January 1864) ↗ reports Lincoln’s reply on the Emancipation Proclamation, and the Fremont (Ohio) Journal repeats it word-for-word a week later.

No text in Lincoln’s own hand is known to carry the line; even sympathetic essays quote it without a citation — America magazine (2015) ↗ builds a reflection around ‘I walk slowly, but I never walk backward’ but gives no origin.
The ‘never walk backwards’ wording most people recognize was popularized by Chief Justice Earl Warren, who made it his favorite Lincoln quotation ↗ from a 1952 Lincoln Day address onward.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular quote strips away the emancipation context
source.excerptNote: As the anecdote appeared in the Daily Commercial Register ↗ (14 Jan 1864) and, verbatim, the Fremont (Ohio) Journal (22 Jan 1864). The circulated version usually drops this framing and often swaps the final word to ‘backwards.’

source.rightsNote: The words themselves — an 1864 newspaper report of a public figure — are long in the U.S. public domain. Note the wording circulates in variants (‘walk back,’ ‘walk backwards,’ ‘walk backward’); the earliest documented form is ‘never walk back.’

author.name: Abraham Lincoln
author.heading: About Abraham Lincoln
author.bio: Abraham Lincoln (1809–1865) was the sixteenth U.S. president, who led the Union through the Civil War and issued the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863. Known for a deliberate, cautious style paired with unbending resolve, he was a natural magnet for aphorisms about patient persistence — some his own, many merely spoken in his voice. This line, tying ‘slow walking’ to never retreating on emancipation, fits him closely, though it reaches us only through the wartime press rather than his own pen.

misattribution.heading: Wording and authorship, sorted out
misattribution.intro: The quote is genuinely and early attributed to Lincoln, so the confusion here is less about who than about the exact words — the version most people know is a later reshaping.

items.why: Chief Justice Earl Warren repeatedly quoted it as ‘I am a slow walker, but I never walk backwards’ — his self-described favorite Lincoln quotation, used from a 1952 Lincoln Day address ↗ onward — and that changed final word is now often presented as Lincoln’s exact wording.

items.who: ‘I walk slowly, but I never walk backward’
items.why: A smoothed paraphrase that circulates widely (e.g. in America magazine ↗) but has no source earlier than the 1864 ‘slow walker…never walk back’ report.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented wording is ‘I am a slow walker, but I never walk back,’ from a January 1864 newspaper ↗ — not the ‘backwards’ version Earl Warren made famous.

context.heading: Why it fits Lincoln
lead: The reported occasion matters. In early 1864, with the Emancipation Proclamation barely a year old and its permanence still contested, Lincoln was pressed on whether the measure was truly final. The newspaper answer — ‘I am a slow walker, but I never walk back’ — reads as a promise that emancipation would not be reversed, even if progress came haltingly.

That is a very Lincoln idea: cautious in pace, immovable in direction. Whether or not he phrased it exactly this way, the sentiment matches the man who inched toward emancipation and then refused to retreat from it.
context.pull: Cautious in pace, immovable in direction.
